meta.description: Berra's documented line, in Newsday (Feb 1986), was "I really didn't say everything I said." The popular "most of the things" wording is a later variant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I never said most of the things I said'?
meta.ogDescription: The joke is Yogi Berra's, the wording isn't. Newsday recorded "I really didn't say everything I said" in 1986; this version is one of five drifted variants.

answer.label: Yogi Berra — but not in these words
answer.authorDates: 1925–2015 · Yankees catcher, manager & Hall of Famer
answer.sourceLine: The joke is genuinely Berra’s, but this is not how he said it. The wording documented in a period source is “I really didn’t say everything I said” — recorded by Newsday on 24 February 1986, when Berra was newly in an Astros uniform. Quote Investigator ↗ lists “I never said most of the things I said” as one of five drifted variants and concludes the support for versions other than the 1986 one is weak; the only dated instance of this exact form it locates is from 2000.
answer.confidenceText: Real Yogi-ism, reworded — the popular sentence is a later variant, not the recorded line.

source.excerpt: “I really didn’t say everything I said,” Berra said, creating another original.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ numbers five variants and reports that in February 1986 “there is good evidence that Yogi Berra did say the first statement above,” recorded in a Long Island newspaper — cited as Newsday (Nassau and Suffolk ed.), 24 February 1986, Sports, p. 92, by Steve Marcus.

The same investigation places the wording asked about here — “I never said most of the things I said” — fifth on its list, with its only dated instance in 2000, in Steven Pinker’s book on language, and concludes: “the support for other versions is weak” (Quote Investigator ↗).
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its Yogiisms section in the “really/everything” form, citing The Yogi Book (Workman Publishing), p. 9 — not the “most of the things” form.
The Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ confirms Berra’s book as The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!, Workman Pub., New York, 1998, 127 pages.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the 24 February 1986 Newsday article, written as Berra was introduced in a Houston Astros uniform. The original article is not freely available online; QI gives the full citation.

source.rightsNote: The wording that can actually be sourced was first published in Newsday on 24 February 1986, and Berra’s own restatement of it appeared in The Yogi Book (Workman Publishing, 1998) — both well after 1930, so both remain under United States copyright. The popular variant “I never said most of the things I said” has no identified originating work at all, which is a further reason not to treat any form of this line as free to reuse.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: About Yogi Berra
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Yankees catcher, manager & Hall of Famer
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra (1925–2015) was a catcher who played nineteen major-league seasons, almost all of them for the New York Yankees, made eighteen All-Star teams and won ten World Series titles as a player — more than anyone in the game’s history. He later managed the Yankees and the Mets and coached for the Mets and the Houston Astros. He is remembered at least as widely for the Yogi-ism: a compact, self-cancelling sentence that turns out, on second reading, to be true. This quote is the genre commenting on itself, which is exactly why so many versions of it circulate.

cite.sourceCitation: Steve Marcus, “Color Yogi a Happy Guy; Now wearing Astros’ rainbow uniform, Berra’s relaxed, popular,” Newsday (Nassau and Suffolk ed.), 24 February 1986, Sports section, p. 92 — cited in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said,” 30 December 2012. The wording recorded there is “I really didn’t say everything I said”; the popular “I never said most of the things I said” is a later variant, the only dated instance of which Quote Investigator places in 2000.

misattribution.heading: The five versions
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this line — the misattribution here is not to the wrong person but to the wrong words. Quote Investigator ↗ lists five circulating forms and finds contemporary support for exactly one.

items.who: “I never said most of the things I said”
items.why: Number five on Quote Investigator’s ↗ list. The only dated instance QI locates is from 2000, in Steven Pinker’s book on language — well after the 1986 report that carries the wording QI can actually support.

items.who: “I never said half the things I said” · “Half the things I said, I never said them”
items.why: Both appear in QI’s chronology ↗ in the 1990s, after the 1986 report, and QI groups them with the versions whose support it calls weak.

items.scope: Word order, even in official sources
items.who: “I didn’t really say everything I said”
items.why: This is how the Yogi Berra Museum ↗ lists it, against the “I really didn’t” order on the cover of Berra’s own book — a small illustration of how freely the sentence moves.

misattribution.truthLine: What Berra was actually recorded saying, in Newsday on 24 February 1986, is “I really didn’t say everything I said” — the wording he later put on the cover of his own 1998 book ↗.

context.heading: A quote about misquotation, misquoted
lead: There is a reason this particular line drifted more than most: it is a joke about people putting words in Yogi Berra’s mouth, and the joke works in any wording. Swap “really/everything” for “never/most” or “never/half” and nothing is lost, so nobody paused to check. Quote Investigator ↗ lays out five circulating versions and can pin only one of them to a contemporary report.

Berra himself leaned into the line rather than correcting it. In 1998 Workman Publishing brought out The Yogi Book, subtitled I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! — the “really/everything” form, on the cover, over his own name (Internet Archive catalogue record ↗). Even so, the word order wobbles in official settings: the Yogi Berra Museum ↗ lists it as “I didn’t really say everything I said.”
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s numbered list of variants runs: “I really didn’t say everything I said”; “I didn’t say everything I said”; “I never said half the things I said”; “Half the things I said, I never said them”; and “I never said most of the things I said.” Only the first is tied to a 1986 newspaper report.

The 1986 remark was made as Berra was being introduced in a Houston Astros uniform; the Newsday piece Quote Investigator cites is headlined “Color Yogi a Happy Guy” and describes him as relaxed and popular in the new job.
context.pull: A joke about being misquoted is the one joke nobody bothers to quote correctly.
